summary: Specifies how to encapsulate and transmit IPv4, IPv6, and ARP packets over InfiniBand. It describes the link-layer address used when resolving IP addresses in IPoIB subnets and how IP multicast addresses map to InfiniBand multicast addresses. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: InfiniBand is a fast road between computers. This says how to put ordinary internet messages into its trucks and how to find the right address.

questions: what is the mtu for ip over infiniband
how does ip multicast map to infiniband
what is the ipoib link layer address
subtitle: How IPv4, IPv6 and ARP packets ride over InfiniBand's unreliable datagram mode, and how its multicast and addresses are mapped.

tldr.problem: InfiniBand is not Ethernet: it has no fixed physical segment, no built-in link addresses of the IP kind, and multicast groups must be created explicitly. IP needs a defined way to run on it.
tldr.mechanism: IP and ARP packets get a 4-octet encapsulation header and travel in InfiniBand unreliable datagrams. A broadcast group defines the link, a 20-octet link-layer address carries a queue pair number and a GID, and IP multicast addresses map to InfiniBand multicast GIDs.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that lets ordinary IP networks be laid over an InfiniBand fabric. It has since been updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 4391 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8064. Check that RFC for the changes to the specification.

sections.title: IP over InfiniBand Datagrams
sections.content:
InfiniBand (IB) defines several transport modes. RFC 4391 picks the Unreliable Datagram (UD) mode, which best matches the needs of IP and is the only transmission method supported by every IB element: routers, Host Channel Adapters and Target Channel Adapters. UD also supports multicasting, partitioning and a 32-bit CRC. All IPoIB implementations MUST support IP over UD. Running IP over IB's other transport modes is out of scope.

The RFC covers laying out an IP network on an IB network, configuring the link, setting up broadcast and multicast, resolving IP addresses and encapsulating IP and ARP packets. It leans on RFC 4392 for an overview of the InfiniBand architecture.
sections.eli5: InfiniBand has several ways to send things. This RFC picks the simple 'toss it over, no promises' way, because every InfiniBand device understands it.

sections.title: The IPoIB Link
sections.content:
An Ethernet link is a physical segment of switches and hubs. An IPoIB link is not. It is an abstract link defined by its members and shared characteristics: the P_Key (partition key), the link MTU and the Q_Key. Two ports using UD can communicate only if they are in the same partition. Several IP subnets may be overlaid on one IB network, and IB subnets can be joined by IB routers into a larger fabric.

Setting up the link centres on the broadcast-GID. It MUST be set up for the subnet to form, and every IPoIB interface MUST join it as a FullMember. The join returns the MTU, the Q_Key and other parameters. The Subnet Manager only allows a join if the node can support the registered MTU, and it ensures members have paths to each other. The broadcast group also gives the link-layer broadcast that ARP and IPv4 broadcasts need.

The RFC recommends that creating and deleting the broadcast group be under administrative control. For the broadcast-GID, the P_Key MUST be a Full Membership key (high-order bit set), a controlled Q_Key with the high-order bit set is RECOMMENDED, and its IB MTU must not exceed any physical link MTU the subnet spans. Local-subnet scope (0x2) is the RECOMMENDED default.
sections.eli5: An IPoIB network is like a club. You belong if you join the club's group chat, and the chat tells you the club rules, like how big a message can be.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Frame Format
sections.content:
Every IP and ARP datagram carried over InfiniBand is prefixed by a 4-octet encapsulation header with two 16-bit fields: Type and Reserved. Reserved MUST be zero on send and ignored on receive. Type holds an Ethernet "ETHER TYPE" number: 0x800 for IPv4, 0x806 for ARP, 0x8035 for RARP and 0x86DD for IPv6.

That header and its IP or ARP payload sit inside the IB frame, between the transport headers and the CRCs. The Global Routing Header (GRH) is required by InfiniBand when multicasting or crossing an IB router, and optional for unicast inside one IB subnet, so an IPoIB implementation MUST handle packets received with or without it.
sections.eli5: Before each message goes in the truck, it gets a small sticker saying what kind of message it is, such as IPv4 or IPv6, so the receiver knows how to open it.

sections.title: MTU and IPv6 Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
IB components support maximum payloads of 256, 512, 1024, 2048 or 4096 octets. The IPoIB-link MTU is the value tied to the broadcast group and can be anything up to the smallest IB MTU along the link. To limit fragmentation and path-MTU discovery trouble, every implementation MUST support an MTU of 2044 octets, which is a 2048-octet link MTU minus the 4-octet encapsulation header. Larger and smaller MTUs MAY be supported.

For IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration, the interface identifier can come from the port's EUI-64 GUID or, when the IPoIB subnet is inside one IB subnet, from a 16-bit LID. LIDs can change after a reboot, so they are poor for persistent addresses. Building the link-local address from the port's EUI-64 is RECOMMENDED. Because the IB spec is unclear on whether a GUID is in modified EUI-64 form, the RFC says: if it already is modified, do not toggle the "u" bit, and if it is unmodified, toggle it.
sections.eli5: Messages have a size limit, like a box that only holds so much. Every device must at least handle boxes of one agreed size, so they can always talk. An address can be built from the device's own serial number.

sections.title: Unicast Address Resolution
sections.content:
IPv4 subnets resolve addresses with ARP and IPv6 subnets with Neighbor Discovery. Sending a packet over IB needs a lot of link information: LID, GID, queue pair number (QPN), Q_Key, P_Key, service level (SL) and path rate. Only part of it travels in the address itself.

The link-layer address is 20 octets: 8 reserved flag bits (zero on send, ignored on receive), a 24-bit QPN, and a 16-octet GID. All IP communication to the interface MUST be directed to that QPN, and including the GID built from the subnet prefix and Port GUID is RECOMMENDED. The other parameters are not carried: the Q_Key from the broadcast group join MUST be used, the P_Key is configured, and LID, SL and path rate come from IBA-approved methods.

In ARP, the hardware type is 32 and the hardware address length is 20. In IPv6, the source and target link-layer address options keep Type 1 or 2 and Length 3, so two zero octets MUST be prepended to fill the 24-octet option. Because the QPN may change across reboots or interface resets, cached entries such as static ARP entries or RARP servers only work if the QPN stays the same, and implementations are RECOMMENDED to revalidate ARP caches periodically.
sections.eli5: An address here is like a home address plus a specific mailbox number. The mailbox number can change when a computer restarts, so it is smart to double-check old addresses now and then.

sections.title: Multicast Mapping and Handling
sections.content:
IB identifies multicast groups with Multicast GIDs (MGIDs), which follow IPv6 multicast address rules. An IP multicast address is combined with the link's P_Key into an MGID: a leading 0xFF byte, flags (the T-flag MUST be 1), scope bits, a 16-bit signature, the 16-bit P_Key, and an 80-bit group ID. The signature is 0x401B for IPv4 and 0x601B for IPv6. An IPv6 group ID is copied into the low 80 bits; an IPv4 group ID is 28 bits, placed in the low bits with the rest zero. The IPv4 limited broadcast address 255.255.255.255 maps to the broadcast-GID.

Multicast in IB differs from Ethernet. A group must be explicitly created through the Subnet Administrator before use, and a sender must join it first. A SendOnlyNonMember join lets a port send but not receive and does not count as a member. A FullMember join also receives. For a group beyond link-local scope with no listeners, the packet goes to the all-router group; if that does not exist, it can be dropped. Senders SHOULD cache group information and MUST subscribe to group create and delete traps. Joined groups MUST use the same P_Key, Q_Key, SL, MTU and HopLimit as the broadcast-GID, and leaving SHOULD be signalled with a FullMember leave request.

IP multicast routers need to hear all groups, but IB has no promiscuous mode. A router can emulate it in software by NonMember-joining every group with an IPv4 or IPv6 signature, and subscribing to creation events to join new ones.
sections.eli5: To send a note to a mailing list, you first have to sign up for it. A computer must join a group before it can send to it or hear from it, and each group gets a special group address.

sections.title: Vulnerabilities and Security
sections.content:
IB multicast operations can fail for resource reasons: creating groups, the join calls and attaching a queue pair. Some failures are hard to notice. If a router fails to NonMember-join a new group, forwarding for that group will likely fail silently. Implementations SHOULD log errors from IB multicast operations, and administrators should reserve multicast resources, for example by using HCAs with ample multicast resources at IP multicast routers.

The Security Considerations section says any multicast network is open to a sender claiming another's identity, forging traffic or eavesdropping, and leaves countermeasures to higher layers. Link setup operations that involve the Subnet Manager and Subnet Administrator MUST be protected by the operating system, and controlled Q_Keys SHOULD be used in all transmissions to stop non-privileged software fabricating IP datagrams.
sections.eli5: Anyone on a shared line might pretend to be someone else, so important secrets need extra locks. Also, if a group signup quietly fails, nobody gets the messages, so computers should write down errors.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: To support ARP over InfiniBand, IANA assigned the value 32 to the Address Resolution Parameter "Number Hardware Type (hrd)" to indicate InfiniBand. Any future use of the reserved bits in the frame format or the link-layer address MUST be published as RFCs, and for now those bits are set to zero on send and ignored on receive.
sections.eli5: A global list keeps track of numbers for each kind of network. InfiniBand got number 32, so everyone can recognize it.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Protocol of the payload, as an ETHER TYPE number.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receive.

fields.name: Queue Pair Number
fields.desc: QP that receives all IP and ARP traffic for the interface.

fields.name: GID
fields.desc: A GID of the port, preferably subnet prefix plus Port GUID.

fields.name: Scope
fields.desc: Scope bits, the same as in the broadcast-GID.

fields.name: P_Key
fields.desc: Partition key of the IPoIB link.

fields.name: Group ID
fields.desc: IP multicast group ID; IPv4 uses only the low 28 bits.
